quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Wolves and Rivers] When wolves were reintroduced to a large national park after seventy years of absence, ecologists expected the elk population to fall, and it did. What surprised them was what happened to the rivers. With fewer elk, and elk behaving more cautiously near open water where wolves could ambush them, willow and aspen seedlings along the banks began to survive. Taller vegetation stabilized the soil, and beavers, which depend on willows, returned to build dams. The dams created ponds, and the ponds provided habitat for fish, amphibians and nesting birds. Some scientists describe this chain of effects as a "trophic cascade" and cite it as evidence that predators shape landscapes. Others urge caution: the park also experienced a decade of unusually wet weather and a rise in bear numbers, both of which could have affected vegetation. The cascade, they say, is plausible but not proven, and the share of the recovery due to wolves alone remains uncertain.
quests.question: Which change directly allowed willow and aspen seedlings to survive?
options: Beavers building dams
A rise in bear numbers
Soil becoming more stable
Elk grazing less near the water
quests.correctAnswer: Elk grazing less near the water
quests.hint: Trace the chain of events back to its first link after the wolves arrived.
quests.explanation: Fewer elk, and elk avoiding open water, let seedlings survive. Stable soil and beaver dams came afterward.
quests.evidenceLine: With fewer elk, and elk behaving more cautiously near open water

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [A Letter, Forty Years Late] Mrs. Whitcombe had retired a decade ago, and the envelope that arrived that Thursday bore a handwriting she did not recognize. Inside was a single page. "You may not remember me," it began. "I was the boy at the back who never finished anything. In your class in 1983 you wrote on my essay, 'Unfinished, but the unfinished part is the interesting part.' I have thought about that sentence for forty years. I am now a structural engineer, and I have a habit, which my colleagues find irritating, of asking what the unfinished part of every plan might be. It has saved us twice from serious mistakes. I wanted you to know." Mrs. Whitcombe read it standing in the hallway, then again at the kitchen table. She did remember the essay, though not the boy. For a long while she sat holding the page, and then she went to find a pen, because she felt that a letter like that deserved an answer, even a late one.
quests.question: What can be inferred about Mrs. Whitcombe's memory of the writer?
options: She remembered him clearly.
She recalled neither the essay nor the boy.
She remembered the essay but not the boy.
She doubted he had been her student.
quests.correctAnswer: She remembered the essay but not the boy.
quests.hint: Read the sentence that begins "She did remember".
quests.explanation: The passage says she remembered the essay, though not the boy, even though the letter reminded her of both.
quests.evidenceLine: She did remember the essay, though not the boy

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Two Reviews and a Reply] Review 1 (five stars): "Spotless room, wonderful staff, and breakfast that made leaving the hotel feel unnecessary. The location is a short walk from the station." Review 2 (two stars): "Our room faced the street and the noise continued until three in the morning. When we asked to change rooms, we were told the hotel was full. Breakfast was good, but sleep matters more." Reply from the manager to Review 2: "Thank you for your feedback. We are sorry that your stay was disturbed. Our records indicate that the hotel was at capacity that weekend because of a festival, and that every room facing the street is subject to noise at these times. We have since added earplugs to all rooms and are exploring thicker glazing. We would be glad to offer you a discount on a future stay in one of our quieter rooms at the back of the building."
quests.question: How do the two reviews differ in what they emphasize?
options: The first criticizes the staff while the second praises the hotel's location.
Both reviewers complain mainly about the breakfast and the staff.
The first focuses on the price; the second on how clean the room was.
The first praises the stay; the second centers on noise and a refused room change.
quests.correctAnswer: The first praises the stay; the second centers on noise and a refused room change.
quests.hint: Compare what each reviewer says first and what they say most about.
quests.explanation: Review 1 is positive about the room, staff, breakfast and location. Review 2 concentrates on street noise and being unable to change rooms.
quests.evidenceLine: the noise continued until three in the morning

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Opinion: Why the Congestion Charge Is Fairer Than It Looks] Opponents of the proposed $8 daily charge for driving into the city center call it a tax on the poor. The objection deserves a serious answer, and the answer begins with who actually drives there. Council data show that only 22 percent of commuters into the center arrive by car, and those who do have a median household income well above the city average. The majority arrive by bus, train or on foot, and they are currently stuck in the same traffic the cars create. The charge would raise an estimated $30 million a year, all of it earmarked for bus services. A fair critique would be that the plan lacks discounts for low-income drivers who have no alternative, and that is a reason to amend the proposal, not to abandon it. It is not a reason to keep a system in which the many subsidize the convenience of the few.
quests.question: What evidence does the writer use to answer the claim that the charge is a "tax on the poor"?
options: Data showing most commuters do not drive and drivers earn more
The writer's own long experience of commuting into the city
A poll of residents' opinions about the proposed charge
Examples from other cities where similar charges failed
quests.correctAnswer: Data showing most commuters do not drive and drivers earn more
quests.hint: Look for the facts that follow the phrase "who actually drives there".
quests.explanation: The council data show few commuters drive and that those who do earn more than average, which weakens the claim.
quests.evidenceLine: only 22 percent of commuters into the center arrive by car

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Home Insurance: What Is Covered] This policy covers loss or damage to your home and its contents caused by fire, storm, flood, theft and escape of water from pipes. Contents are covered up to $40,000 in total, with a limit of $2,500 for any single item unless you have listed it separately on your schedule. Damage caused by gradual wear, poor maintenance, or a failure to take reasonable care is not covered. For example, if a pipe bursts because it was not insulated during a freeze that you knew was forecast, we may reduce or decline your claim. If the home is left unoccupied for more than 30 consecutive days, cover for theft and escape of water is suspended unless you have told us in advance and we have agreed in writing. You must report theft to the police within 24 hours and give us the crime reference number. Claims for items worth more than $1,000 require proof of ownership, such as a receipt, photograph or valuation.
quests.question: A couple's $4,000 watch is stolen. It was not listed on the schedule. What is the most they could recover for it?
quests.hint: Look for the limit that applies to one item that has not been listed separately.
quests.explanation: Unlisted items are covered only up to $2,500 each, regardless of their value.
quests.evidenceLine: limit of $2,500 for any single item unless you have listed it separately

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Island That Wasn't] For more than a century, maps and charts showed a stretch of land called Sandy Island in the Coral Sea. It was marked on British Admiralty charts in the 1870s and, later, in many atlases. In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to the position given and found only deep ocean, more than 1,300 meters deep. The ship's crew checked the charts again, then their instruments, and confirmed that nothing was there. Researchers later suggested that the island's origin was a whaling ship's report from 1876, which was copied from map to map without anyone checking it. Another possibility is that a floating raft of pumice, a volcanic stone that can drift for months, was mistaken for land. Whichever explanation is true, the episode shows how an error, once printed, can acquire authority simply by being repeated, and how rarely anyone returns to check the first source.
quests.question: How was the island's non-existence confirmed?
options: Satellite photographs taken from orbit showed no land there.
A research ship found only deep ocean at the charted position.
Historical documents in the Admiralty archive disproved it.
A whaler's diary was discovered in an old museum archive.
quests.correctAnswer: A research ship found only deep ocean at the charted position.
quests.hint: The confirmation came from a voyage in 2012.
quests.explanation: The vessel sailed to the position on the charts and found deep ocean where the island should have been.
quests.evidenceLine: found only deep ocean

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Interview: A Farmer on a New Crop] Interviewer: You switched to sorghum three years ago. Was that a hard decision? Farmer: Not hard, but not simple either. My neighbors thought I was mad. Wheat is what this valley grows. But the last four summers have been dry, and wheat needs water at exactly the wrong time. Sorghum doesn't mind. It's an old crop in other countries, but around here people hadn't bothered with it for decades. Interviewer: So it was a purely financial decision? Farmer: I'd say it was a decision about risk. Sorghum earns less in a good year. In a bad year, it earns something, and wheat earns nothing. I'm not interested in a crop that makes me rich once and bankrupt twice. Interviewer: Have your neighbors changed their minds? Farmer: Two of them have planted a field each, "to experiment," they say. That's what we call it when we're not ready to admit someone else was right.
quests.question: Why did the farmer choose sorghum?
options: It earns more money than wheat every year.
His neighbors had advised him to plant it.
It is less vulnerable to dry summers.
It is much easier to harvest than wheat.
quests.correctAnswer: It is less vulnerable to dry summers.
quests.hint: Look at what he says about water needs and the last four summers.
quests.explanation: The summers have been dry, wheat needs water at the wrong time, and sorghum is less affected by drought.
quests.evidenceLine: wheat needs water at exactly the wrong time

The neighbors are testing some new farming tools.
The neighbors disagree with his choice of crop.
The neighbors dislike the taste of sorghum.
quests.correctAnswer: The neighbors are quietly following his example.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Fine] When my sister called to ask how the move had gone, I told her it was fine. The boxes had arrived, the movers had been kind, and the new flat had a view of a small park. I mentioned that I had not yet unpacked the kitchen, so I was eating a lot of toast. "Toast," she said. "For how long?" "Only a week or two." She didn't answer immediately. "Do you want me to come over on Saturday? I could bring a casserole. And a screwdriver." I laughed and said that it wasn't necessary, that I was perfectly capable of finding a screwdriver. "I'm sure you are," she said. "Saturday at noon, then." After we hung up, I looked at the stack of boxes labeled KITCHEN and realized I had been waiting, all week, for someone to ask exactly that question. For the first time since the move, I felt the flat might become home.
quests.question: What does the sister realize from the phone call?
options: The move went perfectly and needs no help.
The writer dislikes toast and wants a change.
The writer has nothing left to unpack.
The writer is struggling more than they admit.
quests.correctAnswer: The writer is struggling more than they admit.
quests.hint: Notice her reaction to the word "toast" and her next question.
quests.explanation: The writer says everything is fine but admits to living on toast for a week or two, which tells the sister the move has not been easy.
quests.evidenceLine: so I was eating a lot of toast

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Survey Summary: Remote Work at Calder & Ross] In a survey of 400 employees, 71 percent said they were more productive when working from home. Managers, however, were less convinced: only 38 percent of managers agreed that remote staff produced more. Output figures give a mixed picture. Teams that worked remotely three days a week completed 6 percent more tickets than office-based teams, but the average time to resolve customer complaints rose by one day. The survey also found that 54 percent of employees under thirty said they felt isolated from colleagues, compared with 19 percent of those over forty. The report concludes that remote work benefits individual task completion but may weaken collaboration and the support available to newer staff. It recommends a hybrid model of two office days a week, reviewed after six months, with additional mentoring for staff in their first year. The authors caution that the survey measures perceptions as well as results, and that the figures cover only one department.
quests.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the output figures?
options: Remote work improved every measure that the survey recorded.
Remote work raised task output but slowed complaint resolution.
Remote work reduced task output and complaint resolution.
Remote work had no measurable effect on any of the results.
quests.correctAnswer: Remote work raised task output but slowed complaint resolution.
quests.hint: Read the figures in the sentence that begins "Teams that worked remotely".
quests.explanation: Remote teams completed more tickets but took a day longer to resolve complaints, so the results are mixed.
quests.evidenceLine: completed 6 percent more tickets

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Salary Discussion] Manager: Thanks for coming in, Dev. As you know, budgets are tight this year, so I can't promise anything dramatic. Dev: I understand. I'd like to talk about my role rather than only my salary. Since March I've been managing the onboarding process, which isn't in my job description, and the new hires' completion rates have improved from 70 to 91 percent. Manager: That's impressive. And I appreciate you raising it. I'm glad you came with specifics, because it helps me argue your case with the directors. Dev: I'd like my title and pay to reflect the work I'm doing. I'm asking for a senior grade, which would mean about a nine percent increase. Manager: I can't commit to nine. I could probably do five now and revisit in six months, with a written plan for the senior title. Dev: Five now, plus a written plan with the title agreed by September, and I'll accept.
quests.question: How does Dev strengthen his case?
options: By threatening to leave the company if he is refused
By comparing his pay with what his colleagues earn
By asking for a one-off bonus instead of a raise
By citing a measurable improvement in work beyond his job
quests.correctAnswer: By citing a measurable improvement in work beyond his job
quests.hint: Look at the numbers he gives about the onboarding process.
quests.explanation: Dev points out that he took on onboarding beyond his job description and that completion rates rose from 70 to 91 percent.
quests.evidenceLine: completion rates have improved from 70 to 91 percent
